name: Barcelona
info: Barcelona is a city on the north-eastern coast of Spain, on the Mediterranean between the Llobregat and Besòs rivers, settled by an Iberian people, made the Roman colony of Barcino, later the seat of the Counts of Barcelona and now the capital of Catalonia.

facts.founded: Settlement on the site is older than 5000 BCE; the Laietani, an Iberian people, held Barkeno in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE, and the Romans redrew the town as a castrum about 15 BCE. Founding by Hamilcar Barca or by Hercules is legend.
facts.where: On a coastal plain about 5 km wide on the Mediterranean in north-eastern Spain, between the Collserola range and the sea, and between the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north.
facts.known: The Roman colony of Barcino; a Visigothic royal seat; the County of Barcelona and the Crown of Aragon; a medieval trading port with a large Jewish community; the 1714 siege; the Eixample; Gaudí and Catalan modernisme; the Spanish Civil War; the Olympic Games of 1992
facts.today: Barcelona is the capital of the autonomous community of Catalonia and the second largest city of Spain.

t: Barcelona grew from an Iberian settlement into the Roman colony of Barcino, served as a royal seat of the Visigoths, and from 801 was the seat of the Counts of Barcelona, who became kings of the Crown of Aragon through a marriage in 1137.

After the Catalan institutions took the Habsburg side in the War of the Spanish Succession, its separate status was abolished in 1716, but the port, industry and the Eixample, laid out from the 1850s, made it one of the richest cities of Spain.
It was Republican in the Spanish Civil War, was bombed in March 1938 and fell on 26 January 1939, and under Franco the institutions of Catalonia were abolished; autonomy was restored in 1977.
dyk: On 16 March 1794, although France and Spain were at war, the French astronomer Pierre François André Méchain was allowed into the fortress of Montjuïc to make observations used to measure the distance from Dunkirk to Barcelona, the basis of the first prototype metre.
ev: The Romans redraw the town as the colony of Barcino
The Visigothic king Ataulf holds his court at Barcino and is murdered there
Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, captures Barcelona after a siege of several months
The army of Almanzor sacks the city
Alfonso II becomes both Count of Barcelona and King of Aragon, following the marriage of 1137
The city falls after a siege and assault in the War of the Spanish Succession
Air raids from 16 to 18 March kill more than 1,000 people
More than a million people demonstrate for the restoration of Catalan autonomy, which is granted within a month

sections.origins:
Barcelona stands on a coastal plain about 5 km wide on the north-eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula, bounded by the Collserola range, by the Llobregat river to the south-west and by the Besòs river to the north. The origin of the earliest settlement is unclear. Ruins of an early settlement in the El Raval neighbourhood, with tombs and dwellings, date to earlier than 5000 BCE. In the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE the area was settled by the Laietani, an Iberian people, at Barkeno on the Tàber hill, in the present Ciutat Vella, and at Laie, believed to have been on Montjuïc. Both struck coins that survive, and the name Barcelona comes from the Iberian Barkeno.

Historians have proposed founding stories since the 15th century. One credits the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca, father of Hannibal, with founding the city around 230 BCE. The other credits Hercules, whose crew, after a ship was wrecked off the coast, founded a city called Barca Nona, the Ninth Ship. There is no evidence that Barcelona was ever a Carthaginian settlement or that its ancient name Barcino was connected with the Barcid family, and the northern limit of Punic territory had been the Ebro, over 150 km to the south. A small Greek colony, Kallipolis, has been proposed nearby, but conclusive archaeological evidence has not been found.

The Romans redrew the town about 15 BCE as a castrum centred on the Mons Taber. It was a colony, with a long official name beginning Colonia Faventia Julia Augusta Pia Barcino, which was shortened to Barcino around the end of the reign of Augustus.
sections.growth:
Roman Barcino was a small place. As a colony it was established to distribute land among retired soldiers, and Pomponius Mela listed it among the small settlements near Tarraco, which was far more important. Its position on a branch of the Via Augusta allowed commercial development, and it enjoyed immunity from imperial taxation. In the 2nd century it had a population of 3,500 to 5,000, farmed the land around it and exported its wine widely. The forum's chief building was a temple of Augustus, 35 m by 17.5 m. Under Claudius II, in the later years of the 3rd century, a new double wall with seventy-eight towers was built, the strongest in the province of Tarraconensis, and Barcino grew in importance beside Tarraco.

Under the Counts of Barcelona the city prospered with the growing power of its overlords. In the Crown of Aragon it was by far the largest settlement of the Principality of Catalonia, at least four times larger than Girona, and its economy turned increasingly to trade. In 1258 James I allowed its merchant guilds to draw ordinances regulating maritime trade in the port, and in 1266 he allowed it to appoint consuls to all the major Mediterranean ports. The Taula de canvi, often viewed as the oldest public bank in Europe, was set up by the city magistrates in 1401.

In the 18th century the population grew from 30,000 to about 100,000 as the city became a key mercantile centre of the western Mediterranean. In the 19th century Catalan business interests, many of them based in Barcelona, took part in the Atlantic slave trade: between 1817 and 1867 Catalans were involved in the transportation of 700,000 enslaved people from West Africa to the Caribbean. In 1897 the city absorbed six surrounding municipalities. It had 533,000 people in 1900, and its population peaked in 1979 at 1,906,998.
sections.rulers:
The Roman Republic contested Carthaginian control of the area, and Augustus declared the conquest of the peninsula complete in 19 BCE. In 415 the Visigothic king Ataulf established his court at Barcino, where one of his own troops murdered him. After the defeat of Alaric II at Vouillé in 507 his successor Gesalec moved the Visigothic capital from Tolosa to Barcino, but Ibbas, an Ostrogothic general, defeated him outside the city in 512. Amalaric was murdered by his troops in Barcino, and his successor Theudis ruled from there until 548. The capital was fixed at Toledo in 573.

Moorish forces entered the peninsula in 711, and after the devastation of Tarraco in 717 Barchinona surrendered peacefully and was spared major destruction. Muslim rule lasted roughly 85 years, until Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, took the city in 801 after a siege of several months. Charles the Bald made the Spanish March a hereditary County of Barcelona in 865, and Wilfred the Hairy, appointed in 878, began a hereditary line on his death in 897. Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona, married Petronila of Aragon in 1137, and their son Alfonso II inherited the Crown of Aragon in 1162.

The marriage of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile in 1469 united the two royal lines, and Madrid became the centre of political power. The Catalan institutions sided with the Habsburgs against Philip V, and the last of the Nueva Planta decrees, in 1716, abolished the separate status of Catalonia. Barcelona was annexed to Napoleonic France from 1812 to 1814.
sections.life:
Christian communities in the Tarraconensis date from the 3rd century, and the community of Barcino appears to have been established in the latter half of that century. Saint Cucuphas was martyred nearby under Diocletian, and Saint Eulalia is often considered a martyr of Barcino. The first recorded bishop, Prætextatus, attended the Council of Sardica in 343, and the first major church, the Basílica de la Santa Creu, was built about the end of the 4th century on the site of the later cathedral. The Visigoths formed only a minority of the population, held the positions of authority and were Arians until Catholic Christianity was adopted as the state religion in 589. Under Muslim rule the cathedral was converted into a mosque and taxes were levied on non-Muslims, though religious freedom was largely respected.

A Jewish population is dated from the mid-4th century at the latest. Under the Visigoths Jews suffered discrimination, and Recceswinth's code of 654 outlawed many essential Jewish practices. In the Middle Ages Barcelona had the largest Jewish community in the Crown of Aragon, living in an area called the Call; Montjuïc, meaning Jewish Mountain, was the site of a medieval Jewish cemetery. The city was also the leading centre of the slave trade of the Crown of Aragon until the 15th century, when Valencia overtook it.

In the mid-1850s the density was 856 people per hectare, more than double that of Paris, and the engineer Ildefons Cerdà proposed the Eixample, a grid of streets with wide avenues, gardens inside the blocks and octagonal blocks with chamfered corners.
sections.crises:
In 985 the army of Almanzor sacked Barcelona. The sack was so traumatic that most of the population was either killed or enslaved. The Massacre of 1391 diminished the Jewish community, and the Spanish Inquisition later forced the remaining Jews who refused to convert to burn at the stake or to sell their property and leave. In the late 17th and early 18th centuries the city repeatedly endured war: the bombing of 1691, the sieges of 1697, 1704, 1705 and 1706, and the blockade of 1713 and the siege and assault of 1714.

In the first half of the 19th century the people of Barcelona came into repeated conflict with the Spanish government in the revolts known as bullangues, from 1835 to 1843, which ended with the bombardment of 1842 and the Jamància insurrection of 1843. In the last week of July 1909, called Tragic Week, the working classes, backed by anarchists, socialists and republicans, rioted when reservists were mobilised to fight in Morocco, and over 100 citizens died.

In the Civil War many enterprises were collectivised by the CNT and UGT unions, and much of the city came under anarchist control until the street fighting of the Barcelona May Days. Aircraft bombed the city repeatedly, most severely from 16 to 18 March 1938, when more than 1,000 people died and over 2,000 were injured; the cathedral and parts of the Barri Gòtic were damaged. The city fell into Nationalist hands on 26 January 1939, and a mass exodus of civilians fled to the French border.
sections.legacy:
Roman Barcino survives in the layout of the historic centre, where the Roman grid plan is still visible in the Barri Gòtic, in fragments of the Roman walls built into the cathedral, and in the remains displayed underground at Plaça del Rei by the Museum of the History of Barcelona. The Eixample of Cerdà, imposed by the Spanish government after the city council had given the design of the extension to another architect, became the form of the modern city.

Catalan modernisme left an important legacy between 1885 and 1950. The work of Antoni Gaudí includes the Sagrada Família, under construction since 1882 and financed by private donations; Park Güell, the Palau Güell and Casa Milà were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1984, with four more works added in 2005. The Palau de la Música Catalana and the Hospital de Sant Pau, by Lluís Domènech i Montaner, were inscribed in 1997. Mies van der Rohe's Barcelona Pavilion of 1929 was torn down in 1930, and a re-creation was built in 1986.

Under Franco the use of Catalan in public life was suppressed, and large-scale immigration from Andalusia, Murcia and Galicia followed. After the demonstrations of 11 September 1977 autonomy was restored, and the Olympic Games of 1992 brought the demolition of industrial buildings along the sea-front and the creation of 3 km of beach. Barcelona is now the capital of Catalonia and the second largest city of Spain, with about 1.7 million people.

summary: Barcelona, on the Mediterranean coast of north-eastern Spain, grew from an Iberian settlement into the Roman colony of Barcino and later the seat of the Counts of Barcelona. It became a great port of the Crown of Aragon and an industrial city, and is the capital of Catalonia.
notes: START: no article dates the founding of the city. The main article says the Romans redrew the town as a castrum 'about 15 BC'; the history says only 'at the time of Caesar Augustus' and that the name Barcino was formalised around AD 14. I used -15 with circa true. Settlement on the site is older than 5000 BCE (El Raval) and Iberian Barkeno is of the 3rd-2nd centuries BCE.

1938 BOMBING: the history article says Italian aircraft from Mallorca, 13 raids, 44 tons, 'more than 1,000' dead; the main article says Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, 'at least 1,300' dead. I wrote only 'aircraft', 'more than 1,000' (true on both) and 2,000 injured (both).

AUTONOMY DATE: the main article says Barcelona became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931; the history article says 1932. I left the year out of the text. The main article also says it became capital of the Republic in November 1937; the history article does not; left out.

CATHEDRAL: the main article says the cathedral 'is said to have been founded in 343'; the history article dates the first basilica to the end of the 4th century. I used the history article's date. Prætextatus's attendance at Sardica in 343 is from the history article.

COUNTS: the history article says Wilfred was appointed in 878 and that Charles the Bald made the county hereditary in 865; the sequence as written follows it. Wilfred's death in 897 beginning a hereditary regime is the article's phrase.

ALMANZOR 985 appears only in the main article. The Massacre of 1391 and the Inquisition's treatment of Jews are in the main article only, and its sentence on the Inquisition is garbled ('forced ... to be burned at the stake, or sell their property and leave'); I kept its sense without dates.

The main article says Louis took Barcelona in 801 as 'Charlemagne's son Louis' after a siege; the history says 'several months'. Muslim rule 'roughly 85 years' is the history's figure and does not match 717 to 801 exactly; I kept the article's wording.

The main article gives 'the 17th century Reapers' War' when the city briefly became part of France; no details, left out. The slave-trade passage of the 19th century (700,000 enslaved people shipped by Catalans, 1817-1867) was left out for space but belongs in the editor's reading of the growth of the city.
The main article says the metro was inaugurated in 1924 in a sentence about the 1929 exhibition (history article); an internal inconsistency, so I left the metro out.

Population: 'about 1.7 million' is from the main article, which dates it to 2025; I omitted the year as the guide asks. The history article gives 1,620,943 without a year. Wording of the 1,557,863 in 1970 not used.

The 1992 Olympics and 1987 Hipercor bombing and the 2017 events are told briefly or left out; the Olympic sea-front works are from the main article. I left out the 2017 attack, the referendum, tourism, sport and rankings.

The Hercules legend is attributed in the history article to 'the second myth'; the main article says Greek mythology attributes the founding to Hercules. Phoenician founding 'according to tradition' (main article) was omitted because the history article disputes any Carthaginian presence.
